After that I could only fetch URLs I already had, and none covered 2015-2019. So I have no fetched Composite or Oculus returns, LCH annual or since-inception gains, or firm AUM for 2015, 2016, 2017, 2018 or 2019.
Leads for a follow-up agent (NOT verified, do not use as data):
(a) Bloomberg and Reuters run an early-January article each year on Composite and Oculus returns for the prior year (2016-01, 2017-01, 2018-01, 2019-01, 2020-01).
(b) LCH tables each January (Reuters/FT/Bloomberg/Forbes) list D.E. Shaw with since-inception and annual net gains. Chaining back from verified points ($56.1bn end-2023, implied ~$51.9bn end-2022, implied ~$43.7bn end-2021 if unrevised) gives the earlier cumulative values.
(c) II's Rich Lists for the 2015-2019 years give Composite returns and firm AUM.

Shaw in 2021, which needs confirmation.

The 2026 YTD cutoff for this lens is therefore 2026-09-01 (capital) and none (PnL).

No D.E. Shaw revenue, profit, EBITDA or compensation-expense figures exist in the press; the firm is private and does not publish them. Fund-level dollar sizes for Composite and Oculus are not reported.
evidence.red_flags:
1. Metric confusion. TipRanks reports '$56.1 billion' as D.E. Shaw's 2023 profit, but that is the LCH since-inception figure; the 2023 gain was $4.2bn. Insider Monkey cites 'over $55 billion lifetime net gains', a stale figure. A Quantt guide's '$16 billion profit in 2022' near D.E. Shaw is Citadel's number.
2. AUM bases differ. Reported figures include: $55bn (Dec 2020, of which $35bn alternatives), ~$60bn (2021-2024, a round number repeated for 3 years), >$65bn (Jan 2025), a '$60bn hedge fund platform' (Aug 2025, probably stale boilerplate), >$85bn investment capital (Dec 1, 2025), $72.4bn (LCH/EdR end-2025, probably hedge or alternatives only), and >$100bn / >$115bn 'investment AND committed capital' (Jun and Sep 2026; a wider basis that adds uncalled private commitments). Regulatory AUM is $213bn (SmartAsset/Form ADV, gross and leverage-inflated; never use it as investment capital). A search-engine summary claimed an LCH end-2024 AUM of $41.1bn for D.E. Shaw. I could not find it on any fetched page (it is absent from Navnoor Bawa's article), so treat it as unverified.
3. Return inconsistencies:
- Composite 2021: 18.5% (II) vs 18.8% (Reuters).
- Composite 2022: 24.7% (Bloomberg/Reuters) vs 24.6% (II 2024).
- Oculus 2024: 36% vs 36.1%.
- II's 2021 article labels Oculus's ~15% as '2020' (typo; 2020 was 25.4%).
- Disruption Banking calls 2025 Oculus's best year, which is false (2024's 36.1% was the record).
- Caproasia's summary ordering is ambiguous (third vs fourth); the headline order makes D.E. Shaw third.
4. All annual fund returns are 'people familiar' estimates (Bloomberg/Reuters), not official disclosures. Several syndications (Fortune, Investing.com, Hedgeweek, FA-Mag, Quiver, iTiger, Disruption Banking) recycle one Bloomberg or Reuters report, so they are not independent confirmations.
5. LCH figures are LCH estimates, NET of fees. They probably include gains on internal and employee capital, cover hedge funds only (not the ~$20bn+ long-only/active equity or private vehicles), and are occasionally revised year to year. Chain-checks hold: 79.9 - 67.2 = 12.7 and 67.2 - 56.1 = 11.1.
6. Fee load is high and changes over time. Composite carries a 3% management fee, with its performance fee raised from 30% to 35% (~2022). Oculus's performance fee rose from 25% to 30%. ADV-level maxima are 3.5% management and 40% performance. The gross-up is therefore large and depends on the year.
7. Capital-return policy affects AUM-based estimates. The firm returned half of 2024 profits, virtually all of 2023's, and a 'substantial portion' of 2022's. It returned nothing for 2025 (profits kept in the funds), and capped new money at $2bn into Composite in 2020.
8. The headcount figure ('more than 3,000') may or may not include D. E. Shaw Research and India operations (~1,000 per Rupak Ghose); the website does not specify.
evidence.summary:
This lens covers D. E. Shaw press figures for 2015-2026. Coverage is solid for 2020-2025. Nothing was verified for 2015-2019 because the shared web-search budget ran out (see gaps). There is no 2026 YTD return in the press.

LCH (Edmond de Rothschild) net gains to investors, verified by fetch, are chain-consistent:
- 2022: $8.2bn
- 2023: $4.2bn (cumulative $56.1bn)
- 2024: $11.1bn, #1 for the year (cumulative $67.2bn)
- 2025: $12.7bn, #3 (cumulative $79.9bn)
2020 and 2021 dollar gains were not found. LCH implies ~$21bn combined for Citadel, Millennium and D.E. Shaw in 2021.

Net returns (Bloomberg/Reuters 'people familiar'), Composite and Oculus:
- 2020: 19.4% / 25.4%
- 2021: 18.5-18.8% / ~15%
- 2022: 24.7% / 20%
- 2023: 9.6% / 7.8%
- 2024: 18% / 36.1%
- 2025: 18.5% / 28.2%
- 2025 through end-July: 9.3% / 9.6%

Investment capital: $55bn on 2020-12-01 ($35bn alternatives); ~$60bn in 2021-23; >$65bn in Jan 2025; >$85bn on 2025-12-01. Investment-plus-committed capital, a wider basis: >$100bn on 2026-06-01 and >$115bn on 2026-09-01 (deshaw.com).

Headcount: >3,000 (deshaw.com, accessed 2026-10-08); ~2,500 in older references.

My rough gross-PnL estimates for the orchestrator (hedge-fund PnL before fees, my inference, not sourced):
- **Method:** Gross ≈ LCH net / (1 − blended performance fee on fee-paying capital, ~0.22-0.30, after allowing for ~25-35% internal or fee-free capital), plus management fees of ~2.5-3% of hedge-fund AUM (~$1.0-1.6bn).
- **2025:** ~$18.5bn (range $16-21bn)
- **2024:** ~$16bn ($14-18.5bn)
- **2023:** ~$6.8bn ($5.8-8.5bn)
- **2022:** ~$12bn ($10.5-14bn)
- **2021:** ~$9-12bn (net unknown; Composite ~18.6%, Oculus ~15% on ~$38-42bn alternatives)
- **2020:** ~$8.5-11bn (Composite 19.4%, Oculus 25.4% on ~$33-35bn alternatives, net ~$6-7bn)
- **Long-only/active equity (~$20bn+):** gains are excluded from LCH. They would add roughly ±$1-4bn a year, mostly market beta.
- **2015-2019 and 2026 YTD:** these need follow-up from other lenses or another run with search budget.

evidence.red_flags:
1. Form ADV employee counts (998 for FY2025) are a regulatory subset, not firm headcount. They cover the US umbrella registrant and its relying advisers (London, Asia Pacific, Singapore, Renewables), exclude clerical workers, and exclude D. E. Shaw India and other non-adviser affiliates. Firm-wide headcount is about 3x larger (>3,000). FINTRX and others repeat 998 as the firm's headcount.
2. Regulatory AUM ($213.4B at FY2025, plus $33.4B at D. E. Shaw Investment Management) is gross and leverage-inflated, about 2.5-3x investment capital. Schedule D master-fund gross asset values (Composite $91B, Oculus $56B) are also gross. Do not use them as AUM in the PnL denominator.
3. The capital definition changed. Before 2018 the site reported 'investment capital' ($34-43B, 2014-2017); from 2018 it reports 'investment and committed capital' (~$50B at Dec 2018), which adds undrawn private-fund commitments. The 2017-to-2018 step is therefore partly definitional.
4. Capital jumped from >$70B (Sep 1, 2025) to >$85B (Dec 1, 2025), then to >$115B (Sep 1, 2026). The jump coincided with a redesigned page listing Privates, Active Equity and Multi-Asset. Likely causes include retained 2025 profits (no cash return), the Cogence launch (target $3-5B) and new private funds, but a scope change cannot be ruled out.
5. Entity reshuffles distort ADV trends. D. E. Shaw Investment Management's count fell from 93 to 13 in FY2016. Renewable Investments (111 staff in FY2023) stopped filing separately and became a relying adviser. Direct Capital shrank.
6. Website headcount figures are 'more than X' lower bounds with no as-of date, and they move in steps. The jump from >1,400 (Jun 2020) to >1,700 (Nov 2020) is suspicious. Wikipedia's '2,500 (2022)' is mis-dated; the site said >2,000 until at least Sep 2023.
7. TipRanks presents the $56.1B cumulative LCH figure as 2023 profit.
8. LCH figures are estimates, and they appear to cover only the firm's hedge funds: 2023's $4.2B fits about $45B of alternatives at ~9%, and adding long-oriented gains would far exceed it. Using LCH as firm-wide gains understates the user's all-funds definition, mainly in strong equity years.
9. Quiver Quantitative's 'annualized 12.7% / 13.7%' does not state the period. Hedgeweek/Reuters give 12.9% and 14.4% through 2025, and II gives 12.5% and 12.8% through 2023.
10. The II article on 2023 attributes the 20.1% (2022) figure to an unnamed '2004-launched fund'; this is inferred to be Oculus.
11. Oculus 2024 at 36.1% is reported as its best year ever, consistent with 2022 being 20.1%. Some secondary sources round or mix these years.
12. The 2025 Composite figure (18.5%) is an 'estimate' from people familiar with the fund, not a firm disclosure.

Scope: the D. E. Shaw group, all funds; D. E. Shaw Research PnL excluded.

PRIMARY ANCHORS

- Global headcount (deshaw.com): >1,000 (2014), >1,200 (2018), >1,300 (Dec 2019), >1,400 (Jun 2020), >1,700 (Nov 2020), >1,900 (Dec 2021), >2,000 (Dec 2022 to Sep 2023), >2,500 (Mar 2024 to Dec 2025), >3,000 (Feb 2026 to Oct 2026).

- Alternatives: average alternatives capital x net return, grossed up with an effective 2-3% management fee and 25-35% performance fee. For 2023-2025, LCH net gains are used directly.
- Long-oriented strategies: AUM taken from the 2018-21 site split and the D. E. Shaw Investment Management regulatory-AUM proxy, times benchmark-like returns.
- Range: 5th-95th percentiles. 'All-in gross' matches the task's all-funds, pre-fee definition.
